A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from HPO to DIPPER. Both contain 18 readable pages, including equations, experimental figures, algorithms, and appendices sufficient for reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original robotic simulation results, including success-rate comparisons, subgoal-distance analyses, and hyperparameter ablations.

after.justification: V2 reports original robotic simulation results, including revised benchmark comparisons, subgoal-distance and lower-Q-value analyses, and expanded hyperparameter ablations.

M1.justification: The practical loss in v2 Equation (15) matches v1 Equation (13) after matching the learned lower-value notation. Both algorithms update the lower critic, optimize the higher policy using value-regularized preferences, and train the primitive using SAC. The revised derivation and more explicit critic-update loop do not establish a different practical procedure.

E1.justification: Both evaluate maze navigation, pick and place, push, and Franka kitchen under sparse rewards. Randomized four-room mazes, emphasized in v2's main text, were already documented in v1 Appendix A.5.1. The new discussion of out-of-distribution generalization does not introduce an evaluated task.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 2 adds SAGA and a PIPER ablation without HER. The distance comparison also expands from HIER alone to include the proposed method's No-V ablation, HAC, and RAPS. HPO-FLAT/DPO-FLAT and HPO-No-V/DIPPER-No-V are retained comparators under changed names.

E3.justification: V2 adds average lower-Q values as an evaluation metric and removes the initial/middle/final breakdown of subgoal-distance evaluation. Figure 5 adds lambda settings 5e-4, 5e-3, and 5e-2; Figure 6 adds beta settings 0.2 and 0.4. These expand the evaluation design, while the appendix's network configurations, task horizons, and stated training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 Figures 3–4 analyze subgoal distance during and after training. V2 retains and broadens the distance comparison in Figure 3, replaces the separate final-distance display with a lower-Q-value analysis in Figure 4, and expands parameter-sensitivity evidence in Figures 5–6. The original training-stage analysis is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions report Figure 2 means and standard deviations across five seeds. Neither introduces confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed repeated-training-run count. Revised curves and shaded-band values change results, rather than the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 2 revises several reported curves: kitchen success near 630,000 steps changes from approximately 0.5 to 0.74, while the No-V pick-and-place result falls from approximately 0.09 to near zero. The proposed method's pick-and-place curve is retained. New comparator results, lower-Q values, and expanded sensitivity results substantially change the empirical record.

T1.justification: V2 replaces v1's positive-delta threshold relaxation with an optimality-gap treatment, explicitly formulates entropy-regularized objectives, and rewrites the Bellman derivation using the regularized reward. Section 4.2.2 adds the optimal-value approximation and lower-bound argument leading to the practical loss. These substantially revise the mathematical reasoning despite retaining the practical objective.

C1.justification: The central claims of a bi-level HRL formulation and mitigation of non-stationarity and infeasible subgoals remain. The abstract and introduction raise the claimed maximum improvement from 35% to 40%. V2 also omits v1's explicit introductory claim of autonomously generating preferences through primitive-in-the-loop feedback.

C2.justification: V2 adds limitations concerning generalization to out-of-distribution states/actions and high-dimensional subgoal spaces in Section 6. It explicitly acknowledges practical approximations and interprets high lower-Q values as evidence of feasible, high-return subgoals. These qualify and extend the retained explanation of how the approach addresses HRL instability.

D1.justification: V2 removes v1's operational recipe and reward formula for generating preference labels through primitive-in-the-loop feedback, leaving the feedback source underspecified. It also removes the 100-rollout diagnostic sample count and the statement directing readers to supplementary implementation code. Most hardware, architecture, optimizer, and environment details remain, but the loss of preference-generation instructions materially weakens reproducibility.

R1.justification: V2 adds Harb et al. (2018) and Wang et al. (2023, SAGA), removes Nair et al. (2018), and develops comparisons against SAGA and PIPER without HER. Much of the original related-work discussion is retained in Appendix A.2, so its relocation does not constitute a new literature review.

P1.justification: The title and method terminology change throughout. The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, Section 3 is reorganized into separate hierarchical and preference-learning subsections, baseline discussions are grouped by method family, and the conclusion becomes a discussion with limitations. The original related-work account is largely moved into the appendix.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, expands plot legends and curves, restructures the diagnostic figures, and converts the existing hyperparameter list into Table 1. Typography and page layout change throughout, and existing task visualizations are redistributed. Some labeling defects remain: Figure 3 contains four plots but only three task captions, and diagnostic axes retain HPO labels.

improvement.justification: V2 adds relevant comparisons, broader sensitivity evidence, explicit approximations, and useful limitations. However, it removes the preference-generation recipe and diagnostic sampling details, leaving the feedback source for revised results unclear. Its claim of outperforming PIPER on every task also conflicts with Figure 2's maze comparison. These gains and losses affect central evidence and reproducibility, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
